cowardice_flags.avoided: That after 14 years of s.426(1A) being on the books (in force 1 June 2012), the AG himself described seeking compensation as 'not a conventional practice' of DPPs, and no count of applications or orders exists even months after the April 2026 directive, the provision has functioned as a paper tiger.
cowardice_flags.should_say: The law has existed since June 2012. The AG's own admission that it was not conventional practice, combined with the total absence of published application or order counts before or after the 15 April 2026 directive, shows it has been largely unused in practice. For scam cases the structural limits (ability to pay, foreign masterminds) make it even less effective than the statute suggests.

audience_check: A taxi driver in Ipoh, teacher in Kota Bharu, hawker in Penang, farmer in Sabah or factory worker in Johor would tune out. The cards are precise and sourced but read as a legal technical note on publication gaps. They never translate the gap into the concrete outcome ordinary people experience: billions lost, tiny fractions returned via NSRC, and no visible evidence that courts are forcing convicted offenders to pay victims. It informs specialists; it does not speak to people who have lost savings.

hard_truths_missing.truth: Neither the current Unity government nor previous administrations have published or required publication of s.426(1A) application and order statistics despite the provision existing since 2012. Home Ministry publishes NSRC seizure-return figures (which show low recovery against total losses of RM2.97 billion in 2025 alone); AGC does not publish the parallel court-compensation numbers. Opacity on justice outcomes is bipartisan.
hard_truths_missing.why_avoided: Would require naming institutional failure under both PN-era and current governments rather than stopping at 'no published count found'.

hard_truths_missing.truth: The mandatory language of s.426(1A) ('shall, upon the application of the Public Prosecution') has not produced routine applications. The AG acknowledged it was not conventional practice as of April 2026. No court or AGC publication tracks applications or orders. The 'ability of the convicted accused to pay' factor further limits practical recovery from the low-level mule account holders who are typically the ones convicted in Malaysia.
hard_truths_missing.why_avoided: The analysis correctly reports the absence of a count and the AG's caveat, but does not state the clear implication that the provision has not been operationalised.

class_truths_avoided.truth: Court compensation under s.426(1A) is structurally limited by the convicted person's ability to pay. In scam cases the people convicted in Malaysian courts are frequently low-level mule account holders (young, low-income, or foreign workers) who control little of the stolen funds. Masterminds and the bulk of the money are typically outside Malaysian jurisdiction. NSRC returns of RM7.3 million from RM25.2 million seized (2022-2025) already represent a tiny fraction of total losses (RM2.97 billion in 2025 alone); court orders from mules would recover even less for ordinary victims.
class_truths_avoided.why_uncomfortable: It undercuts the idea that simply getting prosecutors to ask for compensation orders will deliver meaningful recovery. The class position of both typical convicts and typical victims makes the criminal route a weak substitute for prevention or civil recovery against banks/platforms.

predictions.if_nothing_changes: By May 2027 (six months) and by November 2028 (two years) no public count of s.426(1A) applications or orders in scam or mule cases will have been published. NSRC return rates will remain in the low tens of percent of seized funds and a fraction of one percent of total reported losses. Victims will continue to see negligible recovery via either route.
predictions.who_can_fix: Attorney General / AGC (by publishing internal application and order statistics and making them routine); Chief Registrar of the Federal Court or Judiciary (by publishing sentencing and ancillary order data); Parliament (PAC or relevant select committee by requiring the data in annual reports).
predictions.why_they_wont: Publishing low or zero application numbers after 14 years of the statute, and after an AG directive, would document institutional failure. There is currently no political cost for the opacity; Home Ministry can continue highlighting improving NSRC return percentages on a small base.
predictions.label: HYPOTHESIS

cardinal_sin_flags.in_my_attack: Claiming the analysis avoided stating that s.426(1A) has 'never been used'.
cardinal_sin_flags.why_I_dropped_it: The analysis correctly uses 'no published count' and records the AG's own admission that it was not conventional practice. Asserting zero use would require an official answer that has not been given; the stronger defensible claim is prolonged non-use plus continued non-publication.

verification_log.my_attack: s.426(1A) has been in force since 1 June 2012 and uses mandatory 'shall' language upon Public Prosecution application.
AG Dusuki Mokhtar on 15 April 2026 ordered DPPs to apply for compensation and acknowledged it was not conventional practice and not possible in all cases.
NSRC returned RM7.3 million of RM25.2 million seized 2022-2025 (29%) and later cumulative figures around RM14 million against total losses of RM2.97 billion in 2025 alone.
BNM Annual Report 2025 records 969 convictions of mule account holders in 2025.
No published count of s.426(1A) applications or orders exists in AGC, Judiciary, BNM or Home Ministry publications.
verification_log.primary_source: Analysis searches confirmed by independent web search yielding no such statistics.

strongest_card.why: The reframe cleanly contrasts what the Home Ministry does publish (NSRC seizure-and-return figures) against what no one publishes (court compensation order counts under a 14-year-old mandatory provision). It is factually tight and does not overclaim.

weakest_card.why: The mature view correctly identifies the publication gap but stops at 'the public cannot tell whether that law works.' After the AG's own admission that it was not conventional practice and the continued absence of any count, the honest conclusion is stronger: the law has not been operationalised and the opacity continues.

overall_assessment: This is a careful, well-sourced identification of a real transparency failure: a 2012 mandatory compensation provision that the AG admitted was not conventional practice, still has no published application or order statistics months after a 2026 directive, while NSRC return numbers (themselves a tiny fraction of RM2.97 billion 2025 losses) are published. It correctly refuses to invent usage data. Its cowardice is underclaiming. It does not state the plain implication that the provision has been a paper tiger, nor the structural reason court orders will recover little from the low-level mules typically convicted while masterminds and money sit outside Malaysia. Ordinary Malaysians lose money; the analysis explains a gap in statistics without explaining why the gap matters or why institutions have no incentive to close it.
